summary: This document defines a BGP Extended Community that travels with an Ethernet VPN (EVPN) MAC/IP Advertisement route and carries ARP and Neighbor Discovery related flags. With it, a Provider Edge router doing proxy ARP/ND, or ARP/ND on an IRB interface, can answer ARP Requests or Neighbor Solicitations with correct information.

eli5.summary: When someone asks who owns an address, a helper can answer on behalf of the owner if it was told the details beforehand. This document adds a small label so helpers get the details they need to answer correctly.

subtitle: A small BGP tag that lets EVPN edge routers answer ARP and IPv6 Neighbor Discovery requests with the right flags.

tldr.problem: An EVPN MAC/IP Advertisement route does not say whether an IPv6 address belongs to a router or a host, or whether it is an anycast address, so a PE answering on behalf of a remote host may reply wrongly.
tldr.mechanism: A new transitive EVPN Extended Community (Type 0x06, Sub-Type 0x08) rides along with the route and carries a Router (R) flag, an Override (O) flag and an Immutable ARP/ND Binding (I) flag.
tldr.outcome: PEs can answer Neighbor Solicitations with correct R and O flags, and an operator can pin an IP address to one MAC address so that spoofed ARP or NA messages cannot rewrite it.

today: RFC 9047 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2021. It has not been obsoleted or updated, so it is the current definition of the EVPN ARP/ND Extended Community.

sections.title: The Problem With Proxy ARP and ND
sections.content:
In an Ethernet VPN (EVPN), an EVPN MAC/IP Advertisement route can optionally carry the IPv4 or IPv6 addresses tied to a MAC address. Remote Provider Edge (PE) routers use this to fill their ARP or ND tables on IRB interfaces, or their proxy-ARP/ND tables in broadcast domains (BDs). A PE can then answer ARP Requests and IPv6 Neighbor Solicitation messages itself and reduce or suppress flooding.

The catch is that the route may not hold enough information for a correct answer. If a PE learns an IPv6-to-MAC pair through EVPN, it cannot tell whether that pair belongs to a router or a host, or whether the address is an anycast address. That information is simply not in the route.

The RFC fixes this with an Extended Community sent alongside the route. It conveys the flags defined in RFC 4861 so that the answering PE can send Neighbor Advertisement (NA) messages with the correct flag information. It builds on the procedures of RFC 7432.
sections.eli5: A helper who answers questions for others sometimes does not know basic facts, like whether an address belongs to a grown-up or a kid. This document adds a small note so the helper knows.

sections.title: The ARP/ND Extended Community
sections.content:
The document defines a transitive EVPN Extended Community with a Type field value of 0x06 and a Sub-Type of 0x08, as allocated by IANA. It is sent along with EVPN MAC/IP Advertisement routes that carry an IPv4 or IPv6 address.

The community is 8 octets long. After the Type and Sub-Type comes a one-octet Flags field (the third octet), then reserved fields that are set to 0 and ignored by the receiver.

Bits 0-3 and 5 of the Flags field are not assigned. They MUST be set to zero and ignored on receipt.
sections.eli5: It is a tiny label stuck onto a message. The label has a few on/off switches, and the rest of it is left blank for now.

sections.title: The R, O and I Flags
sections.content:
Three flags are defined:

  • R, the Router flag (Bit 7 of the Flags field). When set, the IPv6-to-MAC pair belongs to an IPv6 router. If zero, it belongs to a host. The receiving PE uses it in Neighbor Advertisement messages for that address.
  • O, the Override flag (Bit 6). An egress PE normally advertises IPv6-to-MAC pairs with O set. Only when IPv6 anycast is enabled in the BD or interface does the PE send a pair with O equal to 0. The ingress PE installs the ND entry with the received O flag and always uses that value when replying to a Neighbor Solicitation.
  • I, the Immutable ARP/ND Binding flag (Bit 4). When set, the egress PE says the pair is a configured ARP/ND entry. That IP address can only be bound to the MAC address in the same route, not to any other MAC address received in a route without the I flag set.

The R and O flags have no meaning for IPv4 ARP entries and MUST be ignored when received with a route for an IPv4-to-MAC pair.
sections.eli5: There are three switches. One says 'this is a grown-up router', one says 'my answer should replace what you remember', and one says 'this name always belongs to this exact phone, never change it'.

sections.title: Sending the Community
sections.content:
A PE may learn IP-to-MAC pairs in the management plane, which creates static entries, or by snooping ARP or NA messages from the CE, which creates dynamic entries. These are advertised in MAC/IP Advertisement routes as follows:

  • Routes for IPv6-to-MAC entries MUST include one, and only one, ARP/ND Extended Community with the R and O flag values of the entry. Those values are learned from NA messages or configured for static entries.
  • Routes for IPv4-to-MAC entries MAY include one such community. If they do, the R and O flags SHOULD be set to zero.
  • If a pair is static (configured), the route MUST carry the community with the I flag set.

The community does not change the procedures of RFC 7432, including those for the MAC Mobility Extended Community.
sections.eli5: When a router tells the others about an address, it attaches the label. Addresses that were set up by hand always get the 'never change me' switch turned on.

sections.title: Receiving and Applying the Flags
sections.content:
Only one ARP/ND Extended Community is expected per route. If more than one arrives, the PE MUST consider only the first and MUST NOT propagate the rest. The R, O and I flags MUST be ignored when the route has no IP address.

For R and O: if the route has an IPv6 address and the community, the PE MUST add the flag values to the ND entry and propagate them in Neighbor Advertisements sent in reply to a solicitation. If no community arrives, the PE adds default flags; the default R flag SHOULD be an administrative choice and the default O flag SHOULD be 1.

For I: a PE receiving a route with the I flag set SHOULD install the entry as an immutable binding, which overrides an existing non-immutable binding. Receiving several routes with I set for the same IP but different MAC addresses is a misconfiguration or transient error, and the PE SHOULD update the entry with the latest information. A PE originating an immutable route MAY also set the Sticky/static flag in the MAC Mobility Extended Community, so the binding cannot move either. If two such routes arrive from different PEs, one is selected and the PE MUST alert the operator.

When the I flag is 1, the IP is assumed to be always bound to the same MAC address, so the mobility procedures in [EXTENDED-MOBILITY] for 'Host IP move to a new MAC' do not apply.
sections.eli5: The router that receives a labelled message writes the label next to the address in its notebook. Later, when someone asks about that address, it answers using what the label said. If the label says 'never change', later claims about that address are ignored.

sections.title: An Immutable Binding Example
sections.content:
The RFC gives an example with PE1, PE2 and PE3 attached to the same BD. PE1 originates a route for IP1-to-MAC1 with the I flag set to 1. Later PE2 also originates a route for IP1-to-MAC1 with a higher sequence number and I set to 1. All the PEs in the BD SHOULD keep their IP1-to-MAC1 binding but update MAC1's forwarding destination to PE2.

If PE3 then originates a route for IP1-to-MAC2 with I set to 0, even with a higher sequence number, the PEs do not change their IP1-to-MAC1 bindings. MAC2 SHOULD still be programmed in the Layer 2 BDs. The RFC treats this as a misconfiguration in PE3.
sections.eli5: A name tag that says 'locked' stays on the same person, even if that person moves to another seat. Someone else trying to claim the tag without the lock is told no.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 7432 apply. Proxy-ARP/ND in EVPN BDs may add risk: attackers can use ARP/ND messages to create state in all PEs attached to the same BD and exhaust their resources. Additional mechanisms may be needed, for example limiting the number of proxy-ARP/ND entries per BD or per port, or monitoring the rate at which hosts create dynamic entries.

Wrong flags also cause harm. If an IPv6-to-MAC binding is configured with the wrong R or O flags, every PE in the BD installs and repeats the wrong information. Per RFC 4861, the receiver of an NA with O not set will not update its cache entry, so communication fails. A wrong R flag could add or remove an entry in a Default Router List, so traffic may be sent to a node that is not a router and dropped.

The I flag is a useful security tool. ARP/ND spoofing attacks that inject Gratuitous ARPs or unsolicited NAs with a different MAC address will not succeed in programming the tables, so the spoofer will not receive the traffic.
sections.eli5: A wrong label makes every helper repeat the same mistake. But the 'locked' label stops tricksters from pretending to own someone else's name.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA changed the name of Sub-Type Value 0x08 in the 'EVPN Extended Community Sub-Types' registry to 'ARP/ND Extended Community', referencing this RFC. IANA also created the 'ARP/ND Extended Community Flags' registry, with the I flag at position 4, the O flag at 6 and the R flag at 7. Positions 0-3 and 5 are unassigned. The policy for new entries is Standards Action.

Position 5 is left unassigned and unused because it was previously requested by a separate Internet-Draft, [EVPN-IP-MAC-PROXY].
sections.eli5: A public list keeps track of which switch means what, so nobody reuses the same switch for a different meaning.
